item.title: It’s all downhill from here
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Driving into El Morro campground, I did not expect the road to be blocked by five young girls sunbathing in bikinis, considering this is the middle of nowhere in New Mexico. I’ll swerve to miss a caterpillar, no such manoeuvring is required here as they scurry out of the way and I make the loop [...]
item.content:encoded:
Driving into El Morro campground, I did not expect the road to be blocked by five young girls sunbathing in bikinis, considering this is the middle of nowhere in New Mexico.  I’ll swerve to miss a caterpillar, no such manoeuvring is required here as they scurry out of the way and I make the loop of all 9 spots in the tiny place to return to the only one not taken by the other dozen or so girls…

This is a hell of a campground all of a sudden.  The ranger station at El Morro National Monument up the street told me there was a “group of Germans” staying here.  Why did they not say a German all girls high school?!

Sorry, only nature shots, their chaperones were wary of me enough as is

Haha, sorry to disappoint, but after scurrying over to the next campsite where three of them were at roughly 2 minutes after parking, then hearing they were on a high school trip, that was the end of that.  But they spoke very good English as most Europeans do and had some pretty funny stories as we sat around later in the evening.  Their choice to land in New Orleans and take three weeks to drive through Texas to New Mexico was an interesting one, but of course they could have questioned me the same, and the scenery here truly is one of a kind, which they agreed, so we shared a common mission.

Besides calling a crab “cancer” as in “there were cancers running all over the beach” and me making a WTF face, they did have perhaps the best mistranslation story I have ever heard.  I guess in Germany herb butter is quite common to spread on a piece of bread, but none of the girls knew the word for herb.  So they were at the counter trying to explain it as “we are looking for the special butter with little bits of green in it, you know, the green you grow in your garden in the back”.  This made the store clerk quite uneasy, and me laugh uncontrollably, if they were in California not Texas they probably would have been pointed in the direction of a dispensary.

Just snow melt and rain water, not a spring

Regardless, the title of this post is actually in reference to the fact I just crossed the continental divide.  While I still have to go uphill to get to Santa Fe, that’s by choice, the worst of the hilly portions are behind me, and just as I was starting to master or at least understand Bessie’s change in response at elevation.

Also, thanks to the positive response I got from the video, I already have twice as much raw footage as I did for the first one.  The problem is, I won’t be editing it right away, and I almost don’t want to put up a bunch of picture galleries to ruin the surprise.  Luckily, there is so much insane scenery here in the Wild West, I actually still have to backfill about a week, so that should buy me some time.

item.content:encoded:
OK, after 10 months I guess it’s time for “the video“.  I shot all of it in 1080p for a reason, so trust me it’ll be worth your time if you let it load and watch it on an actual full screen.

I say “the” video, because it takes way too long to shoot and edit to make a habit of this, although I should be able to get it done a little faster next time.  In case you can’t tell, I’ve never made a video before.

I’ve got a million amazing pictures to compile coming up, and in about a week’s time I can explain a little bit of the making of the video, but for now just watch it and react for yourself.

Thanks for following the Blimpster as usual y’all.  Peace.

item.title: I should start selling healing crystals
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: “Which way to the energy vortex?” The fact an elderly couple would approach me at a trailhead in Sedona (gallery here) to ask such a question is somewhat depressing if it means I look like I would know the answer. Although apparently 64% of all visitors to the valley (same number as visit the Grand [...]
item.content:encoded:
“Which way to the energy vortex?”

Yeah! Cuz crystals and aura photography totally exist!

The fact an elderly couple would approach me at a trailhead in Sedona (gallery here) to ask such a question is somewhat depressing if it means I look like I would know the answer.  Although apparently 64% of all visitors to the valley (same number as visit the Grand Canyon) say they come in search of a “spiritual experience”.  I would rate any day that I drove Bessie more than 20 feet and survived a “spiritual experience”, if not every single day over the course of the last ten months, so I guess it depends who you ask.

The story goes that in the early 1980’s, a local woman named Page Bryant came up with the idea while at the hairdressers or under the influence of several gin and tonics, the story differs here and there.  Sorry, when I say “came up with” I mean “had a vision”.  A local clairvoyant clocking in around 400 pounds, she had the brilliant vision that 4 natural energy vortexes could be found in the valley just outside the parking lots of 4 of the already pre-existing highly popular tourist hikes in the area.  And naturally the best way to share this spiritual wealth with the rest of the world would be to sell guidebooks and hire out spiritual tour guides and partner with the largest Jeep tour company in town.

Oh, except for the one she put on the mesa where the airport is.  No matter how clearly marked her maps were, tourists kept wandering onto the tarmac when planes were taking off and landing which made the operator very mad at her, until she had another vision that the vortex had moved near a parking lot slightly down the hill and out of the way.

Spiritual, yes. Bought at a store, no.

Don’t get me wrong though, the red rock cliffs and giant mesas are breathtaking to say the least, and I’m glad I got a chance to see them and hike around, it just kind of drives me watching the nouveau riche either be taken in or attempt to profit from New Age medicine, or religion or whatever bullshit you want to call it when it clearly doesn’t exist.  Of course I did the analysis to see if creating a website selling crap about energy vortexes would be worth the money, and luckily the answer is no.

Still, check the gallery.  And the upcoming 1000 year old Montezuma Castle built into a canyon wall then largest meteor crater in North America are sure to impress.  But not as much as Blimpy the video.  It’s coming Tuesday (once I get close enough to a non-cell phone internet connect).  Look out.

item.title: Album of the Week: King of the Delta Blues by Robert Johnson
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: It’s already shaping up to be a sweltering Texas summer day as Ernie Oertle heads to the door of the American Record Company’s studio in San Antonio to let in his guest, fresh off the overnight train from Jackson, Missouri. It’s 1936 so the Depression is waning and record sales are starting to creep back [...]
item.content:encoded:
It’s already shaping up to be a sweltering Texas summer day as Ernie Oertle heads to the door of the American Record Company’s studio in San Antonio to let in his guest, fresh off the overnight train from Jackson, Missouri.  It’s 1936 so the Depression is waning and record sales are starting to creep back up, but not to the point that the field recording offices are reopening yet.  Ernie doesn’t know a lot about his guest, other than that he’s travelled from a lot farther than Jackson to get here, and that he sounds good.

Robert Johnson walks into the studio with a brooding expression and sets up his chair in the corner facing the wall.  He waits for Ernie to setup one microphone for him to sing into, another next to the mouth of the acoustic guitar he brought along, then immediately breaks into the Terraplane Blues.  Mesmerized by the staccato finger picking of melody and harmony underpinning the passionate, haunted singing, Ernie knows only to do what he does best, let the tapes roll.  “And when I mash down on your little starter, your spark plug will give me fire.”  Primarily a jazz man, Ernie begins to wonder what kind of music this even is, or worse if the man playing it is somehow possessed.

By then the Delta blues were a well established niche, but mostly only with people from the Delta and the plantations where the blues were born.  Kids had grown up hearing of Charley Patton’s late night barn dance antics, or been lucky enough to come across Son House playing on the corner Saturday afternoon.  It was the way to make a living as a travelling musician, a dime here a nickel there, then move on to the next town and the next paying audience.  Because they were such talented entertainers, if a tune was working (people kept dancing, money and liquor kept flowing) they would just keep the riff going, and songs were designed to accommodate this.

But Robert Johnson had a different idea.  Sure, he could keep a crowd going and improvise on a whim, but the title of one track from his San Antonio session is more than telling, The Phonograph Blues.  They say self-awareness is what separates man from beast, so what does it mean when a musician writes songs that are meant to be recorded?  At the time, records were 78 RPM and played one 3 minute song per side.  To use that knowledge to pack as much frenetic energy into as small a space as possible so it will have no choice but to burst back through the needle when played is truly a thing of beauty.

The American Record Company singles proved to be moderate sellers at best, and I doubt Robert Johnson cared much as he delved deeper and deeper into prophecies of his own death two years later at the age of 27.  But for the sound to be immortalized so that not just Ernie Oertle, but the entire world could still hear every flattened third just as it was played 75 years ago is something I care about very much as nothing but a piece of vinyl propels me towards the crossroads.

You can pick this album up at Amazon

item.title: Flagstaff: The only liberal place in Arizona
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Flagstaff is the small artistic liberal university mountain town I expected, and perhaps needed (small enough it only gets a mini-gallery). Same as the expression I’ve heard to describe Austin Texas, the rest of Arizona would probably tell you Flag isn’t part of the state. I’m pretty sure by the end of my two days [...]
item.content:encoded:
Flagstaff is the small artistic liberal university mountain town I expected, and perhaps needed (small enough it only gets a mini-gallery).  Same as the expression I’ve heard to describe Austin Texas, the rest of Arizona would probably tell you Flag isn’t part of the state.  I’m pretty sure by the end of my two days there my CouchSurfing hosts were glad to see me go just so I’d quit trying to discuss politics with them.

Freedom isn't free

They did have a legitimate question why I followed US politics like such a hawk, but I gave my stock glib response that nobody attacks abortion or gay marriage or tries to shut the government down in Canada (actually that last one’s complicated) but generally we’re more the boring type than the complete train wreck type.  Not that we aren’t on the same race to the bottom, it’s just more subtle.  Race to the bottom is also my favourite expression of 2011 so far.

So starting off with the latest and greatest story of #NotIntendedToBeAFactualStatement, I foolishly asked “what State has that poor bastard Jon Kyl as their Senator anyways?”  Naturally the answer was “uhhh…Arizona?”  Oh, whoops, and the other Senator is…oh God, John McCain.  Now I see why people who aren’t Republicans don’t want to talk about it.  Oh well, at least McCain’s authoring the Do Not Track online privacy bill, even though he doesn’t know how to use a computer.

It costs folks like you and me

I alluded to their governor Jan Brewer in a previous post, and felt safe calling her an insane she-devil bitch in Flagstaff.  The forcing police officers to racially profile law that just got struck down by the supreme court was well documented, and illegal immigration is a serious issue here, so their approach is in some fashion at least understandable, if not misguided.  However, when you start piling on all the other bills they keep passing it quickly amounts to right wing insanity, or just plain insanity.  Cutting Medicaid funding for organ donation, making it illegal to teach medical students about abortion, requiring presidential candidates to prove they are US citizens to get on the ballot, passing a bill allowing guns to be carried on university campuses, well, if you Google Jan Brewer the first auto-complete entry that’s not her name is “Jan Brewer recall” which generally isn’t a good sign you’re doing your job.  But she must be listening to reason from somewhere because the two I struck out just got vetoed today.

On the immigration topic I did learn one interesting factoid, there’s a group called Humane Borders that looks into the locations along the Mexican border inside the US where they find the most people dead of dehydration from trying to scramble across the desert, and they go and put water there.  Their point is a good one, wherever you stand on immigration issues, it’s sort of hard to argue in favour of dead people, so may as well take simple steps to prevent that.  Or you could take a page out of the Kansas state rep Virgil Peck’s playbook…can’t wait to visit there!

Oh right, Flagstaff.  Well, the main train line runs through the center of town and there’s one every 15 minutes, their observatory is where Pluto was discovered and the place is at 7500 feet so when I get back there later in the week after Sedona I’m going to hit a golf ball 400 yards.

item.title: Blimpy Gets His Kicks on Route 66
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: The fact that logo in the top left of the page is based off the modern interstate highway sign tellingly places me past the generational divide that worships Route 66. I know it is a road, I know there are blues guitar songs about it. I associate it with diners, chrome and neon. And having [...]
item.content:encoded:
The fact that logo in the top left of the page is based off the modern interstate highway sign tellingly places me past the generational divide that worships Route 66.  I know it is a road, I know there are blues guitar songs about it.  I associate it with diners, chrome and neon.  And having just passed its most famous remaining stretch in Arizona, yup, that’s about all there is to it, rundown nostalgic 50s kitsch (as the gallery shows).

This was my exact picture of Arizona 9 months ago

I say passed, because I only drove on Route 66 for a few miles here or there to stop in some of the silly tourist towns it barely still supports like Kingman and Seligman.  My suspicions against taking the antiquated, less maintained back road were confirmed by white knuckled, violent pothole bouncing along the “new” I-40 that almost has me wanting to write a letter to the State of Arizona as it’s the worst stretch of highway I have seen my entire trip.  Although you get the distinct feeling lack of funds is probably the root of the problem.  The grasp of Vegas is still close enough to take an actual noticeable dent out of the population after I heard a 50 year old man at the laundromat in Kingman griping he was “pretty sure the slot machines were fixed” just before asking the same friend what 9 times 9 was.

I still haven't stopped laughing

I obviously can’t complain to the governor as she’s going to be busy fighting to uphold her racial profiling legislation.  But I did get a little taste of the voters that support her visiting my first Chinese & American food buffet.  Eavesdropping on two fellows at the booth beside me, apparently the census was some sort of government conspiracy to make it seem like there were more Mexicans so they could legitimize immigration.  You have to applaud the angle at least, the census is no more conspiracy than the government itself, especially if you compare it with conspiracy’s dictionary and legal definitions.  Perhaps this is also some sort of insight into why people would root for a government shutdown, I don’t know.

I did manage to learn that Kingman has such a large Chinese population because it was an original railroad town dating back to the 1880s, but now that’s got me questioning exactly what I learned from this Canadian Heritage Moment they used to broadcast when I was 10.  Asian people are explosion proof?  Sorry…still too soon for me to drop a Fukushima joke there…although hopefully you saw that AFLAC needs a new duck because Gilbert Gottfried didn’t think so.  Maybe he should tell the aristocrats joke in a new ad?

Woah, we’re really getting off topic.  Anyways, coming up next Flagstaff and Sedona, the latter of which is the energy vortex capital of the world apparently, so it shouldn’t be too hard to find some liberals under the age of 30.  In the meantime, enjoy the Route 66 gallery.
